topic.title: the siblings' group
topic.claim: The siblings' group without your parents is where the family is actually run.
topic.moment: A decision about papa's surgery gets made in a chat your parents aren't in, before anyone tells them anything.

turn.believed: Your parents are still the ones making the big family calls.
turn.actually: The real decisions now happen in a group chat they can't see, and you present them the result.

topic.because: At some point the children started managing the parents: the money, the health, the logistics. The parent-less thread is where you coordinate the care without worrying them. Power moved rooms quietly.
topic.payoff: The family isn't run from the dining table anymore. It's run from the chat your parents were never added to.
topic.feeling: the strange weight of becoming the ones in charge
topic.villain: the arrangement where caring for parents means deciding over their heads
topic.behaviour: adult siblings coordinate parent care and family decisions in a chat without the parents
topic.mechanism: once kids manage the money and health, the planning moves to a thread parents can't see, so power quietly shifts to them
topic.group: adult siblings jointly caring for ageing parents
topic.send_to: a sibling who's in that exact group chat with you
topic.why_now: year-end health and money decisions cluster in these threads

violations: Slide 6 is a dead slide: it restates the cover's own claim ('decided for them... in a chat they'll never see') almost verbatim as 'run from the chat your parents were never added to' instead of adding a new turn or sting — the last slide repeats the cover's point.
notes: Slide 6: Rewrite the closer so it says something the cover hasn't already said. Right now it's a near-paraphrase of the cover sub ('a chat they'll never see' → 'the chat your parents were never added to'). Give it a new sting — what happens next, or what it costs the sibling who carries it — not a repeat of the premise.

Slide 5: The 'because' is thin — it names the feeling (love, a handover) but not the mechanism. Say plainly why control actually moved to the chat: the kids hold the information and the access now (the reports, the hospital names, the money), so deciding fast without papa lying awake becomes the easier path — and that convenience is also what keeps him out of it. Right now it reads as justification, not explanation.

sources.excerpt: nearly 70% of elderly Indians remain financially dependent

sources.fact: Under Section 80D you can claim up to ₹50,000 per year for health insurance premiums paid for senior citizen parents.
sources.excerpt: up to ₹50,000 per year for health insurance premiums paid for senior citizen parents (aged 60+)

cover.headline: 70% of elderly Indians depend on someone for money. [It's you.]
cover.sub: And they don't know half of what you decide.

paragraphs: 70% of elderly Indians depend on someone for money. It's you.
Your parents' medical report doesn't go to them first. It goes to the sibling group.
The hospital, the doctor, who pays the advance: decided there, without them.
Every one of these chats has typed one line: "Don't tell them the full amount."
Nobody took over. The roles flipped, and nobody announced it.
Call it the parallel family. Same people. One room your parents can't enter.
"Health insurance for parents" is sold to you, not them. Section 80D gives you up to ₹50,000 a year to pay their premium.
Parents get the short version: "Sab set hai."
They don't ask which hospital. The people who decided everything for thirty years take it.
You're not going behind their backs. You're carrying it so they can sleep.
**The family isn't run from the dining table anymore. It's run from the chat your parents were never added to.**

end.send: Send to your sibling in that chat.
end.save: Read it before the next "don't tell them" message.

claims.sentence: 70% of elderly Indians depend on someone for money.

claims.text: Health insurance policies for parents are marketed to the adult children who pay, not to the elderly parents themselves
claims.sentence: "Health insurance for parents" is sold to you, not them.

claims.text: Section 80D of the Income Tax Act allows a deduction of up to ₹50,000 a year for paying a parent's health insurance premium
claims.sentence: Section 80D gives you up to ₹50,000 a year to pay their premium.

sources.quote: Around 70% of elderly in India are financially dependent, either on family or by continuing to work well past retirement

sources.publisher: Kashmir Reader (citing Sankala Foundation/NITI Aayog report)
sources.quote: 70 per cent of India's elderly financially dependent: Report
When you add older parents to a family floater, the premium for the entire policy rises sharply... Your parents' premium stays completely separate from your own plan
Under Section 80D you can claim up to ₹50,000 per year for health insurance premiums paid for senior citizen parents

The maximum allowable deduction for health insurance premiums paid for parents is ₹25,000 in case they are less than 60 years of age and ₹50,000 in case they are senior citizens greater than 60 years of age
